Three adjoining freehold shophouses on North Bridge Road up for sale from $30 mil
article:
A trio of adjoining freehold conservation houses at 742, 744 and 746 North Bridge Road are up for sale through an expression of interest (EOI) exercise. The properties have a combined price starting from $30 million, or $4,000 psf on their total built-up area of about 7,500 sq ft.

The shophouses occupy commercial land totalling 3,734 sq ft, with a street frontage spanning 34 metres.

The ground floor of the shophouse at 742 North Bridge Road, which is a corner property, is approved for restaurant use, while the ground floors of the other two shophouses are approved for F&B takeaway. The properties' upper floors are leased to residential occupants, according to exclusive marketing agent Steward Asia (a team under PropNex).

Located in the historic Kampong Glam area, the properties are close to Haji Lane and Arab Street . They are also within walking distance of Bugis MRT Interchange (East-West and Downtown lines).

Buyers could explore repositioning the shophouses as a boutique hotel, serviced apartments, or a premium hostel, subject to approval from authorities. “Amalgamated ownership across three land parcels provides efficient layout configurations, and versatile options for long-term asset repositioning,”  added Alvin Tan, team lead at Steward Asia.

Meanwhile, URA’s plans for up to 4,000 new private homes in the nearby Kampong Bugis precinct will bring “a new wave of affluent homeowners to Kampong Glam’s doorstep,” said Loyalle Chin, co-founder of Steward Asia. "For these shophouses, that means a larger resident catchment, stronger footfall and resilient rental demand.”

In April, a Government Land Sale site at Kallang Close was awarded to a Frasers Property and Mitsubishi Estate joint venture at $1,415 psf per plot ratio. The site, which can yield around 470 homes, was the first GLS site launched in the Kampong Bugis-Boon Keng-Kallang Bahru precinct in 12 years.

The EOI will close at 3pm on Oct 30.

title: Pair of ground-floor shops in Little India for sale at $9 mil
article:
A pair of adjoining shop units at 28 and 30 Dickson Road in Little India are up for sale via an expression of interest (EOI) exercise. The properties have a combined guide price of $9 million, which works out to about $3,733 psf based on their total floor area of 2,411 sq ft.

Both units are on the ground floor and approved for F&B use, according to ERA Singapore, the exclusive marketing agent. The properties are held on a 999-year leasehold tenure.

They have direct street frontage along Dickson Road and are situated in the Little India-Rochor precinct, which offers a range of dining, hospitality and retail amenities.

The shops are within a three-minute walk from Jalan Besar and Rochor MRT stations.

“The two units may appeal to investors seeking stable rental income from F&B operators, as well as owner-occupiers looking to secure premises in a tightly held city-fringe commercial location,” said Donald Goh, director of capital markets and investment sales at ERA Singapore.

The EOI exercise will close on Nov 3 at 3pm.

title: Can You Eat Your Dividends? (The Curry Puff Strategy)
article:
What if your morning curry puff didn’t cost you a single cent out of pocket?
That is the essence of income investing.
When you invest in reliable
dividend-paying businesses
, the cash flow they generate can directly fund your daily lifestyle expenses – including curry puffs.
But the real secret isn’t just spending your payout right away; it’s choosing what to do with those dividends next.
The Power of Reinvesting Your Snack Money
When your investment portfolio throws off income, you face a classic choice: enjoy the reward today or compound it for tomorrow.
Suppose your dividend payout gives you enough cash to buy four curry puffs.
You could easily eat all four right now.
But if you eat one and reinvest the cash value of the other three back into more shares, your dividend stream expands.
The next time payouts roll around, that growing share count generates even more income – giving you enough for even more curry puffs down the road.
That is
compounding
in action.
You don’t have to lock yourself into an all-or-nothing mindset.
Income investing gives you complete flexibility: if you need emergency funds or want to treat yourself, the cash is there for you to take out.
However, by systematically ploughing a portion of your payouts back into the business, you turn a modest income stream into a compounding snowball.
Pricing Power Beats Inflation
A common worry among retail investors is whether small consumer businesses can survive rising costs.
A single curry puff costs around $2.20 today, but a decade ago, it was notably cheaper.
How does a company navigate
inflation
without ruining its business model?
When input costs rise by 4% or 5%, a company has a few options.
It could make the curry puff smaller or skimp on ingredients, but consumers notice immediately and get upset.
Alternatively, it can leverage its brand loyalty and adjust the price upwards by 10 cents – from $2.20 to $2.30.
Because customers value the product, a small 10-cent price bump doesn’t deter buyers.
That ability to pass modest cost increases onto consumers without sacrificing sales volume is the definition of pricing power.
Over time, companies with strong pricing power can steadily raise prices, defend their margins, and keep growing their dividend payouts to shareholders.
The Only Real Catch
Collecting passive income to buy “free” curry puffs sounds almost too good to be true, so what’s the catch?
The catch is deferred gratification.
There are no free lunches or free curry puffs in the market.
To build an income stream that funds your life later on, you have to forgo spending some of your money today so you can invest it for the long run.
Get Smart: Conviction Beats Market Volatility
Dividend investing bridges the gap between everyday life and
long-term wealth building
.
When you back cash-generative businesses with strong pricing power, you earn the freedom to enjoy your cash today while compounding your future income for tomorrow.

title: How Should Investors Position Their Portfolios for the Rest of 2026?
article:
This article is for educational purposes only and does not constitute financial advice or a recommendation to buy or sell any security. Investors should consider their objectives, financial situation and risk tolerance before investing.
There are only a few months left in 2026, but the investment picture is far from settled. US stocks remain near record highs, earnings have been resilient and enthusiasm around artificial intelligence has held up. Higher bond yields, sticky inflation and geopolitical uncertainty also remain firmly at the fore.
For investors in Asia, the picture is more layered. Different interest-rate cycles, currency moves and sector trends are shaping markets across the region, from semiconductors in Taiwan and South Korea to consumption and manufacturing in Southeast Asia. The question is whether portfolios are positioned for a world where the US still sets the tone while opportunities across Asia become harder to ignore.
Higher Interest Rates Have Changed the Investment Trade-Off
Interest rates remain one of the biggest factors investors need to watch heading into year-end.
On September 16, the US Federal Reserve raised the target range for the
federal funds rate to 3.75% to 4.00%
, saying inflation remained elevated relative to its 2% goal.
Companies may pay more to borrow or refinance debt, while richly valued growth stocks can look less attractive when bond yields rise.
Cash and high-quality bonds, meanwhile, are offering better returns than they did a few years ago. Investors therefore have more choice over where they take risk and where they stay defensive.
What to watch:
Inflation
Central bank guidance
Whether higher interest costs start to eat into company profits
Strong US Markets Still Come With High Expectations
US equities have held up well this year, helped by resilient earnings and continued spending on AI.
The catch is that a lot of optimism is already built into prices. When investors are paying a premium for future growth, even a decent earnings result can fall flat if the outlook is not strong enough.
That is especially true in parts of the technology sector, where valuations have climbed quickly.
Instead of assuming the biggest winners will keep leading, investors may want to ask a simpler question: how much good news is already priced in?
For Asian investors, this matters even more if US technology stocks already take up a large share of the portfolio.
Asia Offers a Different Set of Opportunities
Looking beyond the US does not mean turning away from it. Asia simply offers a different mix of growth drivers, valuations and market cycles.
The
MSCI AC Asia ex Japan Index
covered 996 large- and mid-cap companies at the end of August 2026 and traded at a forward P/E of 10.33 times.
Of course, Asia is not one singular market. China, India, Taiwan, South Korea, and Southeast Asia are all being shaped by very different forces.
While Taiwan and South Korea remain heavily tied to semiconductor and AI demand, Southeast Asia offers more exposure to domestic consumption, manufacturing and infrastructure. Japan, meanwhile, continues to push listed companies to think more carefully about shareholder returns and capital efficiency.
The Tokyo Stock Exchange has kept up its focus on
cost of capital and share price
, with disclosures updated through August 2026.
For investors, the point is not simply to add Asia for the sake of diversification. It is to gain exposure to different sectors, currencies and sources of earnings growth.
Small Caps Still Need a Quality Check
Small caps can offer exposure to niche industries, local consumption and businesses still early in their growth journey. Many also receive less analyst coverage than the region’s blue chips.
Smaller companies, however, have less room for error. Higher borrowing costs can hit indebted businesses harder, while repeated share issuance can dilute existing shareholders.
Take
Multi-Chem Ltd (SGX: AWZ)
. The company released its
latest half-year results
in August 2026 and declared an interim dividend of 16.6 Singapore cents. Rather than treating that alone as a positive signal, investors should still look at cash generation, balance-sheet strength, and how future growth will be funded.
Liquidity matters too. In some Asian markets, getting out of a thinly traded position may not be as easy as getting in.
For small-cap investors, the story matters as much as its numbers.
Rebalancing Can Help Keep Regional Exposure in Check
Portfolios drift over time, even when investors make no changes.
If US technology stocks have outperformed sharply, they may now account for much more of the portfolio than originally intended. Asian holdings, on the other hand, may have become a smaller share simply because they lagged.
Rebalancing
helps bring that mix back into line.
It is not about selling the US because it has done well or buying Asia just to tick a diversification box. Rather, the question is whether the portfolio still reflects the mix an investor actually wants.
For investors based in Asia, a few things are worth checking:
Currency exposure
Home-market concentration
Whether regional holdings genuinely add something different
Rebalancing is really about keeping one region, sector, or theme from quietly becoming too dominant.
What Investors Should Watch Through Year-End
No portfolio will suit everyone. Time horizon, income needs, and comfort with volatility all shape how much risk an investor should take.
Before year-end, it may be worth asking:
Has one stock, sector or market become too large?
Are higher yields creating better alternatives to equities?
Are current valuations supported by earnings?
Does exposure to Asia add something different?
Are small-cap positions strong enough to handle higher borrowing costs?
Is currency risk becoming more important as regional markets diverge?
The US remains a major influence on global markets, but it is not the only source of opportunity.
For investors in Asia, positioning for the rest of 2026 boils down to a few basics: know what you own, understand why you own it, and check whether your mix of global and regional exposure still makes sense today.
